title: Skills and competencies in courses: ideas from other products
intro: This page gathers ideas for setting skills and competencies inside Courses in Essentials 2.0. It compares how other products set up course skills, rubrics, evidence and learner progress. The examples come from the design reference libraries Mobbin and Refero: we kept 25 examples across 12 products. Patterns that sit next to this work, and features the screenshots do not show, are called out. Mapping to scenarios or events, reporting, and Canvas stay in neighbouring modules.

questions.title: Is the framework a central list, free tags, or both?
questions.answer: The screenshots do not settle whether skills come from a central list or free tags. Handshake lets people enter skills and remove them as tags, but the screenshots do not show where the word list comes from or who owns it. Coursera's 'Skills you'll gain' labels state what a course promises; they do not show an instructor picking skills from a governed framework. For Essentials, treat 'institutional competency' and 'course-local skill' as a clear proposed split, with ownership and source visible. Choosing that model is still a product decision; these examples do not prove the market agrees. ClassDojo adds an instructor clue: 'Add skill' and 'Import from' sit together, but the screenshot does not show institutional control or how the import works.

questions.title: How do people search or pick skills when there are hundreds?
questions.answer: Handshake shows typing skills, adding removable tags, saving, and reviewing a shortened set through 'View all'. No suggestion menu appears, so the screenshots do not show autocomplete. ClassDojo gives instructors a small set of controls: categories, skill cards with point values, 'Add skill' and 'Import from', without showing what the import contains. Codecademy helps browse a larger catalog with grouping, sorting and expansion, while Brilliant's four-domain choice stays deliberately small. For Essentials, combine searchable word lists with a lasting chosen set and category context; that mix is a design proposal. Tree selection, handling duplicates, bulk picking and behaviour at hundreds of items still need more evidence.

questions.title: How are levels and rubrics defined: numbers, words, or checklists?
questions.answer: Google Classroom supports building a rubric: criterion and level titles, descriptions, editable points, an optional scoring switch, ordering and 'Save'. Visible shows readable number anchors in a questionnaire people fill in, while Codecademy shows subskill percentages and how skills combine into totals, not a rubric builder. For Essentials, put observable performance wording beside each scoring level, and keep criteria and rating scales editable as one structure. Checklist behaviour, assessor calibration and version history remain open requirements; this set does not prove those patterns.

questions.title: Can you follow a competency through activity, evidence and score?
questions.answer: Codecademy wraps an assessment with the same named subskill, shows answer feedback and an overall result; its 86% result and 85% summary leave it unclear whether the score sticks. Uxcel says an assessment feeds a multi-skill graph and shows reliability, but does not show how each question contributes. ClassDojo shows evidence review and approval, while Kajabi shows assessment setup: each covers a different part of the chain. Essentials should connect a course competency and rubric version to the scenario or event, observation or recording, assessor and resulting score. That full trail is a proposed requirement; none of these screenshots prove it end to end.

questions.title: How do learners see their mastery?
questions.answer: Uxcel gives the most detailed picture: named competencies on a chart, a score, a reliability figure and related learning resources appear together. Codecademy shows individual skill percentages and a Beginner-to-Intermediate progression rule, while its tracking flow mainly reports XP. Brilliant and Duolingo make the current place and the next lesson clear, but those paths do not show assessed mastery. For the Learner Portal, combine a clear next activity with a separately labelled competency level and supporting evidence. Do not treat completion, streaks or XP as mastery without an explicit assessment rule.

questions.title: Can the same competency set be reused across courses and semesters?
questions.answer: Hello Ivy is the only kept example with an explicit save-for-reuse journey. The path is: open a page, open the overflow menu, choose 'Save as template', name and preview it, set personal or shared visibility, then see a save confirmation. It does not show applying a template or how later edits spread. Teachable shows 'Import content', but the source and outcome are missing; treat it as a warning against claiming reusable competency templates from an import button alone. ClassDojo's 'Import from' entry is similarly incomplete. For Essentials, propose an explicit saved competency or rubric set with ownership, preview and target-course selection. Decide separately whether a reused set is a copy or stays linked, how versions are kept, and how old scores still make sense. Reuse of competencies across courses and semesters is not proven by these screenshots.

references.title: Course page shows 'Skills you'll gain'
references.question: Q1
references.take: Coursera shows course skill labels and a 'View all skills' link. This does not show an instructor choosing skills, who governs the list, or assessed competencies.

references.title: Enter profile skills in a dialog
references.question: Q1
references.take: Handshake shows a skills text field, a search icon, guidance to keep the set small, and 'Save'/'Cancel'. The screenshots do not show where the word list comes from or who governs it.

references.title: Review removable profile skill tags
references.question: Q1
references.take: Handshake shows removable skill tags and 'Save'/'Cancel' for a chosen profile skill set. Tags alone do not prove a central list or course ownership.

references.title: Learner picks one of four domains
references.question: Q2
references.take: Brilliant offers four broad domains, a selected choice and 'Continue'. This small single-choice list does not show picking across hundreds of competencies.

references.title: Teacher reviews, imports or adds skills
references.question: Q2
references.take: ClassDojo shows 'Positive'/'Needs work' skill categories, cards with point values, 'Add skill', 'Import from' and family visibility. Search, hierarchy and what the import contains are not shown.

references.title: Browse skill progress and more subjects
references.question: Q2
references.take: Codecademy groups subjects and languages with tabs, sorting, experience points (XP) and 'More available'. That helps scan a catalog, but does not show choosing course competencies.

references.title: Enter and review skills as removable tags
references.question: Q2
references.take: Handshake moves from skill entry to removable tags, 'Save' and a shortened profile set with 'View all'. No suggestion menu or matches from a central list are visible.

references.title: Subskill percentages with Learn and Evaluate
references.question: Q3
references.take: Codecademy shows skill sets, percentage boxes and a subskill panel with 'Builds toward', 'Learn' and 'Evaluate'. This breaks skills into parts and totals them; it is not rubric or level authoring.

references.title: Define rubric criteria, levels and points
references.question: Q3
references.take: Google Classroom combines 'Use scoring', criterion title and description, level title, description and points, add-level and add-criterion controls, sorting and 'Save'. Checklist behaviour and version history are not shown.

references.title: Edit point values in a criterion
references.question: Q3
references.take: A second Google Classroom rubric screen shows a 1-point value and editable level fields, next to the 10-point screen. No scored learner example is shown.

references.title: Health ratings with plain-language meanings
references.question: Q3
references.take: Visible pairs numeric answers with plain-language meanings and 'Submit and calculate score'. It shows readable scale anchors, not instructor-defined competencies.

references.title: Review evidence and approve or return it
references.question: Q4
references.take: ClassDojo shows a learner worksheet response or video and a comment, then 'Approve' or 'Return as draft' and an approved view. That shows a review decision, not a competency score.

references.title: Take a subskill test and see the result
references.question: Q4
references.take: A named Codecademy subskill leads through answered items and correctness feedback to an 86% result. Highest and most-recent scores also appear, but the shown 85% value leaves it unclear whether the score sticks.

references.title: Set up an assessment with auto-grading
references.question: Q4
references.take: Kajabi shows assessment creation, an automatic-grading switch, 'Edit questions' and 'View results'. Captured evidence, computed scores and links to competencies are not shown.

references.title: Assessment result and skill graph impact
references.question: Q4
references.take: Uxcel connects an assessment report and attempt number to six skills, a score, reliability and a timestamp. Help text explains the effect on the skill graph, but per-question contributions are not shown.

references.title: Curriculum path and current topic
references.question: Q5
references.take: Brilliant shows connected topics, a current level, completed, current and upcoming items and a 'Start' action. The path shows curriculum progress, not a validated competency.

references.title: Topic position and lesson counts
references.question: Q5
references.take: Brilliant adds lesson and exercise counts to topic progress. That helps learners find the next activity, but does not show a competency score.

references.title: Mobile curriculum path with a streak
references.question: Q5
references.take: Brilliant combines topic nodes and a next action with a streak banner. Sequencing and engagement are visible; assessed mastery is not.

references.title: Skill percentages and progression levels
references.question: Q5
references.take: Codecademy groups named skills with per-skill percentages and a Beginner level, including how many more skills are needed for Intermediate. Where the assessment came from is not shown.

references.title: Subject tracking that uses experience points
references.question: Q5
references.take: The flow moves from the dashboard to skills tracking, a subject or language summary, an expanded catalogue and a Languages filter. XP bars and learned abilities are visible, but assessment against a rubric is not.

references.title: Lesson path that is not assessed mastery
references.question: Q5
references.take: Duolingo shows unit position, the next lesson, XP and engagement signals. These screens do not show a competency score, rubric level or supporting evidence.

references.title: Mobile lesson path progress
references.question: Q5
references.take: Duolingo keeps the current lesson and upcoming nodes visible on mobile. This is a progression pattern, not evidence of assessed mastery.

references.title: Competency scores, reliability and resources
references.question: Q5
references.take: Uxcel shows six competency axes, a 59/100 score, 40% reliability, peer rankings and resources for a selected competency. How the score is calculated is not shown.

references.title: Save a page as a personal or shared template
references.question: Q6
references.take: Hello Ivy shows 'Save as template', a name and preview, 'For everyone' / 'For me only' visibility and a success confirmation. Applying the template, syncing and version history are not shown.

references.title: Content import is not competency reuse
references.question: Q6
references.take: Teachable shows 'Import content' beside 'Bulk edit' in the curriculum editor. Source, copied fields and result are absent, so competency or rubric reuse cannot be claimed from this screen.
